---
title: "First seen and last seen"
description: "The first and last position report of each track: what they are, and why they cannot be validated."
---

## What it is

Every track has two events that mark where its data begin and end:

- `first_seen`: the first state vector of the track, that is, the first
  position report of the flight received by the OpenSky Network.
- `last_seen`: the last state vector of the track.

The same two times are published in the flight list as the columns
`first_seen` and `last_seen`, and the flight list column `track_duration_min`
is the time between them, in minutes.

These events describe the **reception** of the flight, not the flight itself.
An aircraft is first seen when a receiver first hears it, which can be at the
stand, on the runway or in the air, depending on where the receivers are.

## How it is computed

1. Sort the cleaned state vectors of the track by time (see
   [Trajectory cleaning](trajectory-cleaning.qmd)).
2. The earliest one gives `first_seen`; the latest one gives `last_seen`.
3. Each event takes the position, barometric altitude and measurements of that
   state vector. Its `info` field is empty.

There is no threshold or parameter. Every track has exactly one of each, so the
number of `first_seen` events is also the number of tracks.

## Reference data

None. No reference dataset records when an aircraft was first or last heard by
a receiver network, because that is a property of the receivers, not of the
flight.

## Validation method

Not validated. The events are correct by definition: they are the first and
last state vector of the track. What could be validated is how far they are
from the real start and end of the flight, by comparing `first_seen` with the
off-block time and `last_seen` with the on-block time of the Network Manager's
airport data. That comparison has not been made.

## Results

Not validated.

## Error distribution

Not validated, so no error distribution exists.

Not validated.

## Limitations

- `first_seen` is not the off-block time and `last_seen` is not the on-block
  time. Use the block-time events or flight list columns for those.
- The position in a state vector can be older than its time, because the
  OpenSky Network repeats the last position heard until a new one arrives. In
  three hours of data over Europe, the position of an aircraft's last state
  vector was a median of 190 s old, and more than 30 s old in 55.1% of cases;
  for the first state vector the median age was 0 s. So `last_seen` is often a
  few minutes after the aircraft was really last located.
- The position of either event can be empty where cleaning removed it.
- Both events depend on the track. If a flight is split into two tracks, each
  piece has its own `first_seen` and `last_seen` (see
  [Track identity](track-identity.qmd)).
- They are most useful as a measure of coverage: the time between `first_seen`
  and off-block, or between landing and `last_seen`, is the part of the
  movement that the receivers did not hear.
